subject: Versteylen et al. (1988)
object: Versteylen et al. (1988) described 2 families that appeared to contain examples of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Both families had a striking incidence of severe osteochondritis dissecans of the knees. The authors suggested that the osteochondritis was caused by the fragmented and maldeveloped epiphyses characteristic of epiphyseal dysplasia.

subject: Warman et al. (1994)
object: Warman et al. (1994) mapped the COL9A2 gene, which encodes the alpha-2(IX) collagen chain, to human chromosome 1p32.3-p33 by fluorescence in situ hybridization. Using a single-strand conformational polymorphism within the murine Col9a2 gene, they mapped the mouse gene to chromosome 4.

subject: Warman et al. (1994)
object: Warman et al. (1994) presented new sequence data that completed the coding sequence of the human alpha-2(IX) collagen chain and revised the chicken sequence. This allowed them to compare the carboxyl-terminal NC1 domains of the alpha-1(IX), alpha-2(IX), and alpha-3(IX) chains across species.

subject: Briggs et al. (1994)
object: Briggs et al. (1994) studied a large family with multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Linkage studies with chromosome 19 markers excluded the interval previously linked to PSACH and to a form of MED. Using this family, the authors identified an MED locus (EDM2) on the short arm of chromosome 1, in a region containing COL9A2. This gene encodes the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen, a structural component of the cartilage extracellular matrix.

subject: Briggs et al. (1994)
object: Briggs et al. (1994) excluded the chromosome 19 interval, previously linked to mild and severe PSACH and to a form of MED, in a large MED family that instead mapped to chromosome 1p. This indicated genetic heterogeneity in multiple epiphyseal dysplasia.

subject: Briggs et al. (1994)
object: Briggs et al. (1994) described multiple epiphyseal dysplasia as a dominantly inherited chondrodysplasia characterized by mild short stature and early-onset osteoarthrosis. They noted that some forms clinically resemble mild pseudoachondroplasia.

subject: Muragaki et al. (1996)
object: Muragaki et al. (1996) reported that a mutation in the COL9A2 gene, which encodes the alpha-2 chain of the fibril-associated collagen IX, causes multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (EDM2).

subject: Fiedler et al. (2002)
object: Fiedler et al. (2002) described a 4-generation family of 19 individuals, 12 of whom had a variant of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Starting in childhood, the disease caused pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows and finger joints. Some adult patients had repeated free articular bodies that locked the joint, and affected individuals were prone to early degenerative joint disease. The hips were not markedly affected at an early age.

subject: Fiedler et al. (2002)
object: In the family with EDM2, Fiedler et al. (2002) screened candidate regions and found a new G-to-C change at position -1 of the COL9A2 exon 3/intron 3 splice region, which they thought most likely changes splicing. The change was confirmed by sequencing and by BsaWI digestion in 8 clinically affected family members and in 3 young children who did not yet have symptoms.

subject: COL9A2 G-to-C substitution at position -1 in the COL9A2 exon 3/intron 3 splicing region
Fiedler et al. (2002)
object: Fiedler et al. (2002) used electron microscopy on free articular bodies removed by arthroscopy from 2 patients. Collagen fibril diameter was not obviously different from that of normal articular cartilage. Taking previous reports into account, the authors suggested that mutations causing skipping of COL9A2 exon 3, in the COL3 domain of the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen, may be fairly common in the MED subtype in which the hips are not markedly affected early in life (EDM2).

subject: Nakashima et al. (2005)
object: Nakashima et al. (2005) reported that double-layered patella in multiple epiphyseal dysplasia is not exclusive to DTDST mutation, so this radiographic sign does not by itself indicate the DTDST-related form of MED.
